fullPassage: Carstensen's (1995) socioemotional selectivity theory looks at individuals' goals as a lifelong process that strengthens and matures with ageing. In relation to his motivational conceptual framework, Higgins (2014) proposes that motivation may even attain its highest levels in the later stages of life, subject to the balance and organisation of one's goals in relation to life priorities. Building on this foundation, more recent research looks deeply into additional factors influencing well-being in later adulthood, particularly emphasising the role of self-worthiness, and the overall positive impact of developing a well-rounded self-view during life-course transitions. Taken together, these studies suggest that both goal alignment and positive self-perception are critical in enhancing motivation and overall well-being in later life. Indeed, third-age learners display a higher degree of selectivity in deciding which goals to pursue and how to allocate their resources to those specific priorities. Older adults display a stronger sense of life purpose and self-fulfilment. They do it "their" way, and "their" way is an accumulation of successful and customised combinations in effectively engaging all motivations to varying degrees according to the context of their lives.

Taken together, these studies suggest that both goal alignment and positive self-perception are critical in enhancing motivation and overall well-being in later life. Older adults display a stronger sense of life purpose and self-fulfilment. They do it "their" way, and "their" way is an accumulation of successful and customised combinations in effectively engaging all motivations to varying degrees according to the context of their lives.
